name: Naive cynicism
statement: People expect other people's judgements to be driven by self-interest, and the expectation runs ahead of how self-interested those judgements turn out to be.
meaning: Kruger and Gilovich named the effect for a two-part pattern. Their participants divided responsibility for joint outcomes, then predicted how the other party would divide it. The predictions attributed motivated bias to the other party and not to the self, and they did so whether or not the other party's allocations were in fact biased. The claim is about the accuracy of a forecast, not about whether anyone is self-serving. It is testable in one shape: collect what people do, collect what other people guess they will do, and subtract. Miller and Ratner had run that subtraction a year earlier on self-interest rather than on responsibility, and their version is the one with a preregistered replication behind it.

origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Four studies on married couples, video game players, debaters and darts players. The paper is where the term was attached to the finding; the closely related claim about self-interest was published by Miller and Ratner in 1998.

evidence: The founding article could not be read for this entry. Kruger and Gilovich report four studies in which people divided responsibility for desirable and undesirable joint outcomes and estimated how others would divide it. Their abstract states that participants expected the allocations of others, and not their own, to be motivationally biased, and that this held whether or not the allocations actually were biased. In Studies 3 and 4 participants expected teammates to be less biased than opponents, which the authors read as motivation moderating the effect. That is the whole of what this entry can report about the paper, because the article is paywalled and the abstract was read at OpenAlex rather than at the publisher. Miller and Ratner's five studies are better documented. Their abstract, read at PubMed, reports that participants overestimated how much a financial reward moved their peers' willingness to donate blood, and overestimated how much group membership moved peers' attitudes in Studies 2 to 4 and their behaviour in Study 5. The tendency to overestimate the impact of self-interest on others was largely unrelated to the impact it had on the participant's own attitudes. The original samples were 54 for Study 1 and 81 for Study 4, and no variances were reported, so no effect size can be recovered from them. Brick and colleagues' table of the original descriptives puts the real payment gap in willingness to donate at 10.7 percentage points and the estimated gap at 29.9. Those two figures were read from the replication paper's table, not from Miller and Ratner.

replication.headline: Two preregistered close replications on 1,598 adults reproduced the self-interest version of the claim, while Kruger and Gilovich's own four studies have no repeat this entry could find.
replication.detail: Brick and colleagues ran Miller and Ratner's Studies 1 and 4 in 2019 on 799 United States residents through MTurk and 799 United Kingdom residents through Prolific, ten times the original samples, with both preregistered. In the blood donation study, participants overestimated the effect of a $15 payment by 12.0 percentage points, t(1597) = 23.1, d = 0.58, 95% CI [0.53, 0.63], the two samples giving 0.59 and 0.57. In the smoking study, participants overestimated how far smoking status shifts support for eight smoking restrictions by 19.5 percentage points, t(604) = 19.9, d = 0.81, 95% CI [0.72, 0.90]. Nonsmokers did support the policies more than smokers, on 13 of 16 tests, so the estimates were stretching a real difference rather than inventing one. Dropping the 5.5% of ratings recorded as 'no opinion' cut the smoking overestimate to 12 percentage points. Both results were classed as signal in the same direction as the original, and neither could be compared with the original for size, because Miller and Ratner reported no variances.

study.cite: Brick, C., Fillon, A., Yeung, S. K., Wang, M., Lyu, H., Ho, J. Y. J., Wong, S. C., & Feldman, G. (2021). Self-interest is overestimated: Two successful pre-registered replications and extensions of Miller and Ratner (1998). Collabra: Psychology, 7(1), 23443.

limits: No repeat of Kruger and Gilovich's four studies was located. Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, Unpaywall, PubMed and general web search returned citing work and no repetition of the responsibility allocation design, and Brick and colleagues do not cite the paper at all. The article itself is closed: Unpaywall records no repository copy, PsycNet and ResearchGate refuse the request, and the abstract quoted here came from OpenAlex. The clearest opposing result is Epley and Dunning's. Across four studies they found that people overestimate their own generosity while predicting others fairly accurately, which puts the error in self-prediction rather than in cynicism about others. Brick and colleagues write that their results appear to contradict that paper, and suggest the difference lies in immediacy, since cynical expectations may be correct where the consequences are concrete. Their own caveats matter as much. The measures were self-reported willingness and policy support rather than observed behaviour, and they note that the pattern is equally consistent with accurate estimates and inaccurate self-reports. Policy endorsement ran near ceiling in Study 4. Both samples were Western. Communal orientation, tested as a moderator of overestimation, predicted nothing, r(797) = -.02, p = .53 in Study 1 and r(397) = .02, p = .72 in Study 4. The extension grading smoking status five ways drew 15 light, 18 moderate and 6 heavy smokers, too few for a test.
misreadings: Naive cynicism and naive realism are separate claims from separate groups, and this site carries them separately. Naive realism, as Ross and Ward set it out, is a stance about one's own perception being an unmediated reading of events. Naive cynicism is a forecast about what drives other people's judgements, and someone can make that forecast without holding the stance. The effect is also not a finding that other people are unbiased. Kruger and Gilovich's abstract says the expectation of motivated bias appeared whether or not the allocations were biased, which makes the claim one about calibration. Miller and Ratner's smokers did oppose smoking restrictions more than nonsmokers, and the estimates put that gap well above where it sat. Nor is the pattern confined to hypothetical questionnaires. Martuza, Thorbjørnsen and Sjåstad pooled 31 belief-behaviour comparisons from 11 experiments in which participants could lie anonymously for money, N = 8,126, and found beliefs about others' dishonesty running 13.6 percentage points above the behaviour, g = 0.61. Giving managers the real honesty rates reduced their support for surveillance and other freedom-restricting measures, N = 741. Those figures were read from the authors' preprint abstract.
